title: Ultimate China Travel Guide 2026: First-Time Visitor's Complete Handbook
description: Everything you need to know before visiting China in 2026 - from visa-free policies and mobile payments to transportation, language tips, and the best cities for first-time visitors.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# Ultimate China Travel Guide 2026

Welcome to your complete handbook for visiting China in 2026. This guide covers everything from the new visa-free policies to the apps you absolutely need before you land.

## Visa-Free Entry: What Changed in 2026

China has dramatically expanded its visa-free transit and mutual exemption agreements. Citizens of 50+ countries can now enter China visa-free for periods ranging from 7 to 30 days. Check the latest list before booking.

## Mobile Payments Are Now Foreigner-Friendly

The biggest myth about traveling in China is that you need cash. In 2026, Alipay and WeChat Pay both accept international credit cards directly. Link your Visa or Mastercard in the app, verify with passport, and you can pay anywhere - from street food vendors to high-end restaurants.

## The Apps You Must Download Before Landing

- **Maps**: AMap or Baidu Maps - Google Maps doesn't work reliably in China
- **Translation**: Baidu Translate or iFlytek - both work offline
- **Ride-hailing**: DiDi - the Chinese Uber
- **Metro**: App-specific to each city, but most support English
- **VPN**: Download and configure before arriving

## Best Cities for First-Time Visitors

1. **Beijing** - The Great Wall, Forbidden City, and Peking duck
2. **Shanghai** - The Bund, art deco architecture, and futuristic skyline
3. **Xi'an** - Terracotta Warriors and 3,100 years of history
4. **Chengdu** - Giant pandas and Sichuan cuisine
5. **Guilin** - Karst mountains and Li River cruises

## Transportation: The 4-Layer System

China's transportation is world-class once you understand the system:

- **High-speed rail**: The fastest way between major cities (350 km/h)
- **Domestic flights**: For distances over 1,500 km
- **Metro systems**: Available in all major cities, all signposted in English
- **DiDi**: Ride-hailing that works without speaking Chinese

## Cultural Etiquette Essentials

- Bring a small gift if invited to someone's home
- Don't stick chopsticks upright in rice (resembles funeral incense)
- Use both hands when giving or receiving business cards
- Tipping is not customary and can cause confusion

## When to Visit

The best months are April-May and September-October. Avoid Chinese New Year week unless you specifically want to experience it (everything closes, but the festivities are unmatched).

## Ready to Plan Your Trip?

Browse our 35 city guides for deep dives into specific destinations. Each guide includes neighborhood breakdowns, must-eat restaurants, hidden gems, and a local's perspective.

---

*Have questions? Ask our [ChinaGuide AI](/ai) for personalized recommendations based on your travel dates, budget, and interests.*

title: How to Pay in China 2026: Alipay, WeChat Pay & Cash for Foreigners
description: A practical guide to mobile payments in China - how to set up Alipay and WeChat Pay with your foreign credit card, plus what to do when digital payments fail.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# How to Pay in China 2026

China is the world's most cashless society - but until recently, foreign visitors were locked out. Here's how it works now.

## The Big Change: Foreign Cards Work

As of late 2024, both Alipay and WeChat Pay accept international Visa, Mastercard, and other foreign credit cards directly. Setup takes about 5 minutes.

## Setting Up Alipay

1. Download Alipay from your app store
2. Tap "Tour Card" or international version
3. Add your credit/debit card
4. Verify with passport scan
5. Set a 6-digit payment PIN

You can now pay at:
- Convenience stores (7-Eleven, FamilyMart)
- Supermarkets
- Restaurants
- Taxis and DiDi
- Most tourist attractions

## Setting Up WeChat Pay

WeChat Pay works similarly:

1. Install WeChat (the messaging app)
2. Open "Me → Services → Wallet"
3. Add a foreign card
4. Complete identity verification with passport
5. Enable payments

## When Mobile Payments Don't Work

Always carry some cash as backup:
- 500-1000 CNY is enough for emergencies
- Use Bank of China, ICBC, or HSBC ATMs
- Avoid independent ATMs with high fees

## Tax Refund for Tourists

When shopping over 500 CNY at participating stores, ask for a tax refund form. At the airport, present forms, receipts, and goods at the tax refund counter before departure.

## Money-Saving Tips

- Use credit cards with no foreign transaction fees
- Avoid currency exchange at hotels (worst rates)
- Bank ATMs in China typically give better rates than airport exchanges

## Common Payment Mistakes

1. **Don't try to use Google Pay or Apple Pay** - They don't work in China
2. **Don't share QR codes with strangers** - This is how scams work
3. **Check the merchant name** before confirming payment

---

*For city-specific payment tips and recommended apps, see our [Payment Guide](/guide/payment).*

title: 5 Best Cities in China for First-Time Visitors (2026 Edition)
description: If this is your first trip to China, these five cities offer the perfect mix of iconic sights, food, and infrastructure. We've added 2026-specific tips and seasonal advice.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# 5 Best Cities for First-Time Visitors

China is vast - 9.6 million square kilometers - and choosing where to go can be overwhelming. After surveying thousands of travelers, here are the five cities that consistently delight first-time visitors.

## 1. Beijing - Where History Meets Power

**Why visit**: The Forbidden City, Great Wall (Mutianyu section), Temple of Heaven, and Peking duck.

**Best for**: History buffs, families, anyone who wants to understand modern China.

**Days needed**: 4-5

**2026 tip**: The Forbidden City now requires advance booking 7 days ahead. Tickets sell out during summer weekends.

## 2. Shanghai - Art Deco and Skyline

**Why visit**: The Bund, French Concession, Yu Garden, and the world's second-tallest building.

**Best for**: Foodies, architecture lovers, nightlife enthusiasts.

**Days needed**: 3-4

**2026 tip**: The new Suzhou Creek walking path connects the historic waterfront areas - perfect for a half-day stroll.

## 3. Xi'an - 3,100 Years of History

**Why visit**: Terracotta Warriors, ancient city walls (you can bike them), Muslim Quarter street food.

**Best for**: History enthusiasts, food lovers.

**Days needed**: 2-3

**2026 tip**: Visit the Terracotta Army early morning (8 AM) to avoid tour bus crowds. The on-site museum has been renovated.

## 4. Chengdu - Pandas and Sichuan Spice

**Why visit**: Giant Panda Base, Sichuan cuisine capital, teahouse culture.

**Best for**: Animal lovers, foodies, slower-paced travelers.

**Days needed**: 2-3

**2026 tip**: Panda Base requires advance reservation. Morning visits (7:30-10 AM) are best for active pandas.

## 5. Guilin - Karst Mountains and River Magic

**Why visit**: Li River cruise, Reed Flute Cave, Longji Rice Terraces.

**Best for**: Photographers, nature lovers, families.

**Days needed**: 3-4

**2026 tip**: The Li River cruise from Guilin to Yangshuo is best booked 2-3 days in advance, especially April-October.

## Suggested Itinerary: 10 Days

- Days 1-4: Beijing
- Day 5: High-speed train to Xi'an (4.5 hrs)
- Days 5-6: Xi'an
- Day 7: Fly to Guilin
- Days 7-9: Guilin + Yangshuo
- Day 10: Fly to Shanghai or return home

## Don't Try to See Everything

The biggest mistake first-timers make is cramming too much in. China rewards depth over breadth. Choose 3-4 cities max, spend 3-4 days each, and you'll have a far richer experience than racing through 8 cities.

---

*Browse our complete [City Guides](/cities) for deeper information on each destination.*

description: Practical 2026 travel tips for Xi'an: best time to visit Terracotta Army, Muslim Quarter food, City Wall bike rental, and visa-free entry for foreign visitors.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# Xi'an Travel Tips 2026

Xi'an blends 3,100 years of imperial history with modern high-speed rail access. This guide covers the essentials for a first visit in 2026.

## Top five things to do
- Reserve the Terracotta Army morning slot a day ahead (opens 08:30).
- Bike the Ming City Wall at sunset (full loop is 14km).
- Eat biang biang noodles in the Muslim Quarter before noon.
- Watch the Big Wild Goose Pagoda fountain show at 21:00.
- Visit the Shaanxi History Museum on a Tuesday to avoid the Monday closure.

## Getting around

Metro Line 2 connects the North Railway Station to the City Wall in under 30 minutes. Taxis via Didi work in English; have your hotel write the destination in Chinese before boarding.

## Visa-free entry in 2026

China's 30-day visa-free policy now covers France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Malaysia, and Switzerland. Carry your passport and hotel reservation when you arrive at Xi'an Xianyang International Airport (XIY).

China's 240-Hour Visa-Free Transit: 57 Countries in 2026
description: Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam joined on Aug 20, 2026 — 57 countries, 65 ports. What the rule really allows, and four mistakes that get people turned around.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# China's 240-Hour Visa-Free Transit in 2026: What Actually Changed

A colleague flew Frankfurt → Shanghai → Bangkok last month with a 9-day gap in the middle. She'd read that China's transit visa-free stay was "240 hours" and assumed she was fine. At Pudong immigration, the officer asked for her onward ticket to Thailand. She had it. She was through in about four minutes.

Her seatmate on the same flight was not. He had a round-trip Frankfurt → Shanghai → Frankfurt ticket, which is not a transit — it's a return trip. He was sent to the visa-on-arrival counter and spent two hours there.

The rule is generous. The paperwork is where people lose.

## What the 240-hour policy actually is

China's transit visa-free program lets citizens of 57 countries enter without a visa for up to 240 hours (10 days), provided they are genuinely in transit to a third country or region. As of **August 20, 2026**, Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam were added, bringing the list from 55 to 57 countries. The number of eligible entry ports also rose from 60 to 65, with new points at Guangzhou, Hengqin and Zhongshan in Zhuhai, the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, and West Kowloon Station on the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong Express Rail Link.

That last one matters more than it sounds. West Kowloon is the station where the Express Rail from Hong Kong clears mainland immigration inside the building. Adding it as a transit port means you can now fly into Hong Kong, take the train to Shanghai, and use the 240-hour rule — you don't have to fly into a mainland airport first.

## 2026 is the year visa-free stopped being a niche

Visa-free entry accounted for **77.7 percent of all foreign arrivals** into China in the first half of 2026, according to reporting by The Diplomat in August. That's not a policy footnote anymore; it's the main channel.

Two separate programs are doing the work, and confusing them is the single most common error:

| Program | Stay | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| **Unilateral visa-free** (45+ countries) | 30 days | Ordinary passport from an eligible country. No onward ticket needed. Valid through Dec 31, 2026. |
| **240-hour transit visa-free** (57 countries) | 10 days | Confirmed onward ticket to a **third** country. Enter/exit through approved ports. |
| **24-hour transit** (most nationalities) | 24 hours | Stay inside the airport transit area, or hold an onward ticket if leaving it. |

Canada and the UK joined the unilateral list on **February 17, 2026**. If you hold one of those passports, you may not need the transit rule at all — check the 30-day list first. Most people I talk to are using the harder program when the easier one already covers them.

## The four mistakes that get people turned around

**1. Round-trip tickets are not transit.** Shanghai → Beijing → Shanghai is a domestic loop. The rule requires you to exit to a *different* country or region than the one you arrived from. Hong Kong and Macao count as third regions, which is why so many itineraries route through them.

**2. "240 hours" is a cap, not a promise.** The clock starts at 00:00 the day after you enter. Your permitted area also depends on which port you use — the 240-hour rule allows travel across 24 provinces, but not all of them from every entry point. Landing in Kunming does not automatically let you fly to Harbin.

**3. The onward ticket must be confirmed, not "planned."** Immigration officers ask for the booking. A screenshot of a search result is not a ticket. Airline staff at your departure airport may also refuse to board you if they can't see a confirmed onward segment — this happens more often than the actual Chinese border check.

**4. Nationals of some countries are excluded even within the 57.** The list is by nationality, not by passport type, and it changes. The National Immigration Administration publishes the current list; third-party blogs (including this one) go stale. Check before booking.

## What to have ready at the counter

Print or have offline on your phone:

- The confirmed onward ticket with a date inside 240 hours
- Your hotel booking for the first night (they rarely ask, but it's a one-second look)
- The arrival card, filled in before you reach the desk
- The name of the port you're entering — officers occasionally ask which transit point you're using

That's it. There's no application, no fee, no pre-registration. You walk up, they stamp, you go.

## Where the policy is heading

China's 15th Five-Year Plan explicitly commits to "orderly expanding" the unilateral visa-free list and "optimizing" transit arrangements. The direction is one-way: more countries, more ports, longer stays. The August 2026 additions were the third expansion in eighteen months.

If your country isn't on either list yet, the trend suggests it eventually will be. If it is on the list and you're still applying for tourist visas, check the rules again — you may be doing paperwork you no longer need.

## Sources

1. [National Immigration Administration — Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam added to 240-hour transit (Aug 20, 2026)](https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147413/c217834/content.html)
2. [China Briefing — China Visa-Free Travel: Complete Guide (65 ports)](https://www.china-briefing.com/news/china-visa-free-travel-policies-complete-guide/)
3. [Visas Update — China 240-Hour Visa-Free Transit: 57 Countries, 65 Ports (Aug 22, 2026)](https://www.visasupdate.com/post/china-240-hour-visa-free-transit-57-countries-2026)
4. [Trip.com — China Visa-Free Transit 2026: 24/240-Hour Rules](https://us.trip.com/blog/china-visa-free-transit/)
5. [The Diplomat — China's Tourism Gains Momentum Thanks to Visa-Free Policies (Aug 2026)](https://thediplomat.com/2026/08/chinas-tourism-industry-gains-momentum-thanks-to-visa-free-policies/)
6. [National Immigration Administration — List of Countries Under Unilateral Visa Exemption](https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183390/content.html)

## Frequently asked questions

### Q1: I hold a US passport — can I enter in Shanghai and leave from Beijing?

Yes. The 240-hour rule allows entering and exiting through different ports, provided you are ultimately travelling to a third country or region (Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan count). Shanghai in, Beijing out, then fly to Seoul — fully compliant. You must declare your itinerary on arrival, and your travel area is limited to 24 provinces.

### Q2: Should I use the 240-hour transit or the 30-day visa-free entry?

If your passport is on the 30-day unilateral visa-free list (45+ countries, including Canada, the UK, Japan, South Korea and Australia), use that instead — no third-country ticket required, and a wider travel area. The 240-hour transit rule exists for travellers whose countries aren't on that list, or whose trip is genuinely a transit. Plenty of people use the clumsier programme when the simpler one already covers them.

### Q3: My route is Shanghai → Beijing → Shanghai. Does that count as transit?

No. That's a domestic round trip. The rule requires your onward destination to differ from where you arrived. Shanghai in, Shanghai out to the same country — does not qualify. Shanghai in, Hong Kong out — qualifies, because Hong Kong counts as a third region.

### Q4: When does the 240-hour clock start?

At 00:00 the day after you enter, not the moment you land. Land at 14:00 on 10 March and your 240 hours run from 00:00 on 11 March, so you must leave by 24:00 on 20 March. Those extra hours are routinely overlooked.

### Q5: Do I need a visa for the third country?

No third-country visa is required — but you do need a confirmed ticket. A German passport holder flying Frankfurt → Shanghai → Bangkok only needs the confirmed Bangkok segment. Whether Thailand is visa-free for them has no bearing on the Chinese rule.

### Q6: Why was I stopped at the airline counter?

Usually because ground staff cannot see a confirmed onward ticket, or its date falls outside the 240-hour window. Airlines are liable for boarding passengers who fail entry requirements, so they are often stricter than Chinese border control. Save the confirmation as an offline PDF the moment you book — you need it at check-in and at the border.

### Q7: Which ports accept 240-hour transit?

As of August 2026, 65 ports — including Shanghai Pudong/Hongqiao, Beijing Capital/Daxing, Guangzhou Baiyun, Shenzhen Bao'an, Chengdu Tianfu, Kunming Changshui, Hangzhou Xiaoshan and Xi'an Xianyang, plus the new Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, Zhuhai Hengqin/Zhongshan and West Kowloon Station. Always confirm against the National Immigration Administration's own list; third-party summaries go stale fast.

title: China Visa-Free Entry Ends 31 Dec 2026: Your 2027 Playbook
description: 48 countries lose 30-day visa-free entry on 31 Dec 2026. Russia runs to 2027. What changes for Spring Festival 2027 trips, and the routes that still work.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# China's Visa-Free Entry Ends on 31 December 2026

The question arriving in our inbox most often this month, from Melbourne to Munich: *"I booked flights for Chinese New Year 2027 — am I still fine?"*

If your passport is on the list below, the honest answer is no. Not unless something changes in the next seven weeks.

China's 30-day unilateral visa-free entry runs to **31 December 2026, 24:00 Beijing time**. The National Immigration Administration publishes the country list; the visa application centres publish the end date. Both are current as of this writing on 11 November 2026, and neither contains a 2027 date.

This is the part most travel content skips: the deadline is not the only thing expiring. A second, quieter deadline falls on the same day, and it hits your wallet rather than your boarding pass. And there is one passport in the group that has already been given an extra year — a detail that has been reported almost nowhere.

Here is what actually changes, what still works, and the four mistakes that will cost people a trip in the first quarter of 2027.

## What expires on 31 December 2026

Ordinary passport holders from 49 countries can currently enter China without a visa for business, tourism, family visits, exchange visits, or transit, for stays of up to **30 days**. The clock starts at 00:00 on the day *after* you enter, not on your landing day.

| Region | Countries |
|---|---|
| Europe | 35 — including the UK, Schengen states, Russia, the Nordics, and the Balkans |
| Asia | 7 — Japan, South Korea, Bahrain, Brunei, Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia |
| Americas | 6 — Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Peru, Uruguay |
| Oceania | 2 — Australia, New Zealand |

The Japan and South Korea entries surprise people who last checked in 2023. So does Canada and the UK, both added on 17 February 2026. The list is genuinely broad — which is exactly why so many 2027 itineraries were built on the assumption that it is permanent.

It is not permanent. It is a trial arrangement with a printed end date, and that end date is 31 December 2026.

### One passport group already has 2027 covered

Russia is the exception, and it is a real one. The official notice lists Russia separately with its own validity: **until 31 December 2027**.

So the accurate framing is 48 countries expiring at the end of 2026, plus Russia running a year longer. If you hold a Russian ordinary passport, the December deadline does not apply to you yet. Everyone else on the list is in the same boat.

## The second deadline on the same date: the visa fee

This one gets almost no coverage, and it matters if you end up applying for a visa in January.

Chinese embassies and consulates in the United States are running a **reduced fee schedule that is itself valid only until 31 December 2026**. For US citizens that means $140 for a single-entry, double-entry, or multiple-entry visa — including the 10-year multiple-entry tourist visa. The same $140 buys the ten-year version, which is why the per-trip maths on a ten-year visa is not close.

For non-US citizens applying in the US, the reduced fees run $23 single entry, $34 double entry, $45 for a six-month multiple, and $68 for twelve months or more. Express service adds $25.

Both the fee reduction and the visa-free scheme were extended to the same calendar date. What the fee schedule looks like on 1 January 2027 has not been published. If you are going to need a visa anyway, applying in December 2026 is cheaper than applying in January 2027 — and cheaper again than applying in a panic.

## Three bookings that break

**A trip that straddles New Year.** Enter on 30 December 2026 and you are assessed under the rules in force that day, which should give you the full 30 days and put you out on roughly 28 January 2027. That is the reasonable reading of a visa exemption granted at the border — but it is a reading, not a written guarantee, and airline check-in systems that validate documents (Timatic and its equivalents) are notoriously slow to reflect edge cases. If your entry date is 31 December, expect questions. If it is 1 January, do not board without a visa.

**Chinese New Year 2027.** The State Council published the 2027 holiday schedule on 5 November 2026: Spring Festival runs **5 February to 13 February 2027**, nine days, with Chinese New Year's Day itself on Saturday 6 February. The two working Sundays are 31 January and 14 February. That whole window sits six weeks *after* the visa-free scheme lapses. Every hotel, train, and flight inside that window will be at its annual peak, and everyone arriving from a listed country will need a visa in their passport first.

**Anything in January or February involving snow.** Harbin, Chongli, Yabuli, the ski bits of Xinjiang. None of these touch the deadline itself, but they all sit in the post-deadline months, and they are the trips most likely to be booked late and cheaply, then discovered to be unboardable.

## What still works after 31 December 2026

The deadline does not close China. Three routes survive it, and one of them is nearly as generous as the scheme that is ending.

### 240-hour visa-free transit

Nationals of **57 countries** — including the US, UK, and Russia — can transit through China without a visa for up to **10 days**, entering via any of **65 ports across 24 provinces**. Requirements: an ordinary passport plus an onward ticket with a confirmed seat and a confirmed departure date. Inside the permitted area you can travel, do business, visit family, and move between cities.

The catch is the word *transit*. Your itinerary must be A → China → C, where C is a third country. Flying home to the country you came from does not qualify. This route was never part of the December deadline, and it has no published end date.

### Hainan's 30 days

Hainan Province runs its own regional scheme under completely separate rules: **61 countries**, up to **30 days**, no visa, for tourism, business, family visits, medical treatment, conferences, and sports events. The list is broader than the mainland equivalent — it includes the United States, the United Kingdom, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Mexico, and Kazakhstan, none of which are on the mainland 30-day list.

The limitation is geographic. You must enter and stay within Hainan. Fly to Shanghai from Sanya on day three and you are out of status. If a winter beach is the actual goal, Hainan works; if the Great Wall is the goal, it does not.

### A normal tourist visa

Unfashionable, unglamorous, and currently cheap. See below.

## If you need a visa, here is the real timeline

For US applicants the process runs through the online COVA form, then an appointment at a visa application service centre, then a decision.

- **Fee:** $140 for US citizens, any number of entries, any validity — the ten-year multiple-entry visa costs the same as a single entry.
- **Processing:** 4 business days for regular service; express is 2–3 business days for an extra $25.
- **Validity:** US citizens are generally issued the ten-year multiple-entry tourist visa by default.

Four business days sounds comfortable until you add the two things that actually eat the calendar: appointment availability at the centre nearest you, and the mailing time each way if you are not applying in person. During the run-up to Spring Festival, appointment slots in major cities disappear weeks out. If your trip is inside 5–13 February 2027, start the application in December 2026.

## Four mistakes that cost people the trip

**Treating the 240-hour transit as a general backup.** It requires a third country. A London → Shanghai → London round trip fails the test. A London → Shanghai → Tokyo trip passes it.

**Confusing Hainan with the mainland.** Hainan's 30 days do not transfer. The island is the whole permission.

**Counting the arrival day as day one.** The 30-day clock starts at 00:00 the day after entry. Land on 1 December and your last day is 31 December, not 30 December. Getting this backwards by a day at the end of a trip is the single most common overstay.

**Waiting for an announcement instead of booking a refundable flight.** The policy has been extended before — the current end date is itself the product of a November 2025 extension notice. It may well be extended again. But "may well be" is not a document you can show at a check-in desk, and an extension announced in late December leaves no time to obtain a visa before a February departure.

## Frequently asked questions

**Does the 31 December 2026 deadline apply to Russian passports?**
No. The official notice lists Russia separately with validity until 31 December 2027. Russians holding ordinary passports have another year of 30-day visa-free entry.

**Will China extend the visa-free policy again?**
Not announced as of 11 November 2026. The policy has been extended repeatedly, and the current end date came from an extension published in November 2025 — roughly eight weeks before the previous expiry. If the pattern holds, an announcement would land around late October to mid-November 2026. There is no way to book a February 2027 trip on a pattern.

**My trip starts 28 December 2026 and ends 10 January 2027. Do I need a visa?**
Under a straightforward reading, no — you are assessed at entry, and entry happens while the scheme is in force. But your onward travel and the airline's document check both need to agree with that reading. Carry a printed copy of the NIA country list and the end date, and confirm with your airline before ticketing.

**Can I use the 240-hour transit to visit China and then fly home?**
No. The itinerary must continue to a third country or region. Returning to your country of departure disqualifies you under the transit rule.

**Is Hainan a workable alternative for a winter trip in January 2027?**
Yes, if the plan is beach and resort rather than Beijing and Xi'an. Sixty-one nationalities get 30 days visa-free, and the scheme has no published end date. You cannot leave Hainan for the mainland on it.

**How long does a Chinese tourist visa take in practice?**
Four business days of consular processing for regular service, two to three for express. Add appointment lead time, which is the variable that catches people — during Spring Festival season, book the appointment before you book the flight.

**What is the actual difference between the 30-day entry and the 240-hour transit?**
Thirty days, any port, no onward ticket, 49 countries — expiring 31 December 2026. Ten days, 65 designated ports, onward ticket to a third country required, 57 countries — no published end date. The second scheme is narrower on time and looser on nationality.

## Sources

- [National Immigration Administration — List of Countries Covered by Unilateral Visa Exemption Policies](https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183390/content.html) (compiled as of 17 February 2026)
- [National Immigration Administration — Visa-Free Transit Policies](https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183412/content.html) (updated 20 August 2026)
- [National Immigration Administration — Regional Visa-Free Entry Policies](https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c180637/content.html) (updated 20 August 2026)
- [Chinese Visa Application Service Center — Notice on Visa Exemption Policy](https://visaforchina.cn/BER4_EN/tongzhigonggao/552368139170615339.html) (26 August 2026)
- [Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the United States — Notice on Extension of Visa-Fee Reduction](https://us.china-embassy.gov.cn/eng/lsfw/zj/notice/202412/t20241227_11519914.htm) (29 December 2025)
- [Xinhua — State Council General Office notice on 2027 public holidays](http://www.xinhuanet.com/20261105/ac6792e1565949dc8e7d6e8261b9a055/c.html) (5 November 2026)

*Planning around the deadline? Read our breakdown of [how the 240-hour transit rule actually works](/blog/china-240-hour-visa-free-transit-2026) and [how to pay for things once you are through immigration](/blog/china-payment-guide-2026).*

title: Harbin's Ice Season Has Started. The Park Has Not.
description: Snow-making started 18 Nov for Harbin's 28th Ice and Snow World. What is confirmed, what is not, and the transit-visa line that ends at the city border.
author: ChinaConnect Editorial Team
content:
# Harbin's Ice Season Has Started. The Park Has Not.

Two emails landed this week. One from a couple in Utrecht who booked flights to Harbin for 8 January and want to know when tickets go on sale. One from a photographer in Osaka who asked, in one line, "is the park open yet?"

Both got the same answer, and neither liked it. As of 19 November 2026, the 28th Harbin Ice and Snow World has published neither an opening day nor a 2026-27 ticket price. What has already started is everything around it: the machines, the province's event calendar, and the booking sites that are now selling dates nobody has confirmed.

Here is what is solid, what is not, and how to book without guessing.

## What is actually confirmed

- **18 November 2026**: snow-making started at the park itself. The operator says more than 30 snow machines are running around the clock, and the first batch of snow goes to a large "Snowman Family" sculpture outside the east ticket hall.
- **2 November 2026**: the Heilongjiang provincial government announced the frame of the 2026-27 ice and snow season. It runs from early November 2026 to March 2027, close to five months, with more than 30 headline events, over 100 ice and snow themed activities, and ten suggested routes.
- **7 December 2026**: the traditional ice-harvesting ceremony on the Songhua River, held on the "Major Snow" solar term, opens the cultural half of the season. The 43rd Harbin Ice and Snow Festival ceremony follows as the centrepiece.
- **The venues named for this winter**: the 28th Ice and Snow World, the 39th Sun Island International Snow Sculpture Expo, the 9th Songhua River Ice and Snow Carnival, and the 53rd Zhaolin Park Ice Lantern Fair.
- **6 November 2026**: Yabuli ski resort opened. The resort now runs 56 pistes across its linked three-mountain system, with lifts upgraded for this season.

Notice what is missing from that list: a date you can build a flight around. The provincial announcement describes the season's frame, not the park's opening day, and those are not the same thing. Chinese winter parks open when the ice is thick enough and the structures pass inspection, which is a physical constraint, not a marketing decision.

## The ticket price you will find online belongs to last winter

The operator's own site, checked today, still shows the price table for the **27th** edition: 328 yuan for a standard adult ticket, 240 yuan for concessions. That is a real, official number. It is also last season's number.

Treat it as a planning anchor, not a quote. When the 28th edition publishes, expect the figure to move, and expect an early-season discount window like the ones run in previous years. Before you pay anything, check three things: which edition the listing names, whether the date you are buying is inside that edition's operating window, and what the refund rule is if the park delays opening.

Official sales run through the park's WeChat channel. If you cannot complete WeChat Pay verification with a foreign card, international resellers are a legitimate fallback, but you are paying a markup for someone else to hold the booking, so read the cancellation terms before you click. Bring the passport you booked under. Chinese attractions and railway stations increasingly check the document tied to the reservation.

## The transit visa rule that ends at the city line

This is the part that quietly ruins itineraries, and almost no English-language guide spells it out.

China's 240-hour visa-free transit, as published by the National Immigration Administration and updated on 20 August 2026, covers 57 countries arriving through 65 ports in 24 provinces. In Heilongjiang there is exactly one such port: Harbin Taiping International Airport. So the flight works.

The stay area does not. For Heilongjiang, the permitted area is listed as Harbin City, not the province. That matters because the two headline side trips sit on opposite sides of that line:

- **China Snow Town**, at Shuangfeng in Hailin, is roughly 280 kilometres southeast of Harbin and belongs to Mudanjiang. It is outside the transit stay area. Entering on the transit waiver and going there is overstaying.
- **Yabuli** is in Shangzhi, which the Harbin municipal government administers. On paper that keeps it inside the stay area, but this is exactly the kind of edge case to confirm with the officer at the counter rather than with a blog post, mine included. Ask, get the answer, and keep the boarding passes and hotel bookings that show your route.

Two more conditions people forget. You need a confirmed onward ticket to a third country or region, not back home. And if your passport is on China's 30-day unilateral visa-free list, that scheme expires on 31 December 2026, which we broke down separately in [our visa deadline guide](/blog/china-visa-free-deadline-december-2026).

The scale of transit traffic into Harbin is not small. In the first year of the policy, the airport handled over 600,000 arrivals and departures, including 180,000 foreign nationals and more than 60,000 visa-free entries, up 285.3 per cent year on year. Officers at that counter have seen the questions before.

## Getting to the park without the taxi argument

Harbin Metro Line 2 has a station named after the park, which makes the metro the simplest answer on a clear night. If you take a taxi, the operator publishes reference fares on its own site: about 20 yuan from Central Street, about 24 yuan from the museum area in Nangang, about 26 yuan from the Chinese-Baroque district, and roughly 50 minutes from the airport, which is 39 kilometres out.

Save those numbers. "The meter is broken" stops working when you can quote the official reference, and if it escalates, the park's service line is 400-639-1999, staffed 9:30 to 21:30. Ride-hailing works across the city too; check the plate before you get in.

## The cold is a logistics problem, not a warning

Harbin's January average is minus 18 degrees Celsius. That is not a footnote for your packing list, it is the single constraint that shapes the day.

Phones die in the cold, so keep yours inside your coat, not in an outside pocket, and carry a power bank you keep warm as well. Two pairs of gloves beat one expensive pair, because you will take one off to use a screen. Boots need room for a wool sock, since tight boots are cold boots. Plan outdoor stretches of around 90 minutes and use the warming halls between them. And if you are visiting at night for the lights, remember that the night is also the coldest part of the day; the queue for the big slide is where people regret their footwear.

Payment is the other logistics piece. Alipay and WeChat Pay both accept foreign cards now, but set them up before you fly, not at a ticket window in minus 20. Our [payment walkthrough](/blog/china-payment-guide-2026) covers the setup order.

## Dates that will eat your trip

The State Council published the 2027 public holiday schedule on 5 November 2026. Spring Festival runs from 5 to 13 February 2027, nine days, with the Lunar New Year's Eve on 5 February. Harbin's domestic peak lands on that window and the week on either side of it. Hotel rates in the city do not creep up in that period, they step up.

If you want the sculptures without standing shoulder to shoulder, aim at the last week of December, after the ice harvest and once the park has found its rhythm, or a midweek day in late January. Avoid the first week of February entirely if you can move.

One more timing note: this park is built from river ice. It closes when the ice starts to go, usually in late February or early March, and the closing date is announced, not scheduled a year ahead. Do not book a March trip around it.

## Four expensive mistakes I keep seeing

1. **Booking flights around "5 January".** That was the opening ceremony date of the previous edition. It is a reasonable guess, not an announcement.
2. **Buying a "skip the line, includes transport" bundle at three times gate price.** Check the gate price against the operator's own table first, then decide whether the transport is worth the difference.
3. **Booking a Harbin hotel for the Snow Town leg.** It is 280 kilometres and a different prefecture. Either move hotels or take the long day trip, but do not assume a taxi at 6am.
4. **Planning a transit-waiver trip across three provinces.** The 240-hour clock is generous, the geography is not. Read the stay area for your entry port before you build the route.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Harbin Ice and Snow World open right now, on 19 November 2026?**
No. Snow-making began on the evening of 18 November, which is the first construction step, not the opening. The operator has not published an opening day for the 28th edition.

**How much will a 2026-27 ticket cost?**
Not published yet. The 27th edition was 328 yuan standard and 240 yuan concession. Use those as a reference, and confirm the edition label on any listing before paying.

**Can I use the 240-hour visa-free transit to visit China Snow Town?**
Not on the transit waiver. The permitted stay area for Heilongjiang entries is Harbin City, and Snow Town is in Mudanjiang, about 280 kilometres away.

**What about Yabuli? Is that inside the stay area?**
Yabuli is in Shangzhi, which Harbin administers, so it plausibly sits inside the area. This is a case to confirm at the border counter with your itinerary in hand rather than assume from a guide.

**Do I need a visa if my passport is on the 30-day visa-free list?**
That scheme ends on 31 December 2026. After that date you need a visa, the transit waiver, or Hainan's separate 30-day entry. Details are in [our deadline breakdown](/blog/china-visa-free-deadline-december-2026).

**When is the quietest week?**
After the Spring Festival holiday ends on 13 February 2027, or a midweek day in late January before the holiday traffic builds. Early February is the busiest stretch of the season.

**Is it worth going if the opening date is unconfirmed?**
Yes, if you can keep the park day flexible. Book refundable accommodation, put the park in the middle of the trip rather than the first day, and check the operator's channel the week you fly.

**Do I need to speak Chinese to manage the park?**
Not strictly, but the official ticket channel is inside WeChat, and the service line is in Chinese. Have a translation app ready, screenshot your booking, and keep the park's address in Chinese characters on your phone for taxi drivers.
